utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case Number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you follow what I'm saying in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Yes, I can follow you in the language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please sit down. Appearances, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you all. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with David Cunningham and Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you. I understand there is a follow-up on a point that was raised yesterday by Mr. Ackerman, by myself actually in the first place, with regard to the statements or interviews of -- with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Your Honour, can I very briefly run through the background to this, although I think Your Honour will probably remember it. Your Honour, the interviews in this form by way of tape-recorded -- tape-recordings, some of which were interviews conducted as -- with the interviewee as a witness, and some as a potential suspect. Your Honour, these interviews began in July of 2001, all of them virtually were by summons issued by the Prosecutor. Your Honour, the purpose of those interviews was quite simply to see whether any of the people who had intimate knowledge of the events and the institutions in that they were Bosnian Serbs would be able to assist potentially as witnesses for the Prosecution or at the lowest, to provide information which would be of assistance to the case. Now, Your Honours, the Defence were aware of this throughout. And when the -- we reconvened in September of 2001 for a Status Conference, the matter was raised by Mr. Ackerman, then supported, I believe, by Mr. De Roux before Judge Hunt in the Status Conference. Your Honour, the order then was to notify the Defence of the Rule 68 material contained in those interviews, and that, I checked -- is the transcript of that Status Conference at page 355. Now, Your Honour, the matter was raised again in the Status Conference before Your Honour on the 16th of January of 2002, I think shortly before the trial began. And there, I think, Your Honour, it was -- can I just check. I've made a reference for this. But -- yes, Your Honour, I think this is the important point that Mr. Ackerman was talking about yesterday. Your view to me was that it was a commitment on my part that anything which needed to be disclosed under Rule 68 would. And I then -- I said this: "I want to make it absolutely clear, we are not going to disclose the full transcripts. We are going to disclose the Rule 68 material." And your reply to that was "you made that clear last time." I think you were referring to the Judge Hunt Status Conference, and I think it was taken as that is how it should be. And Your Honour, what then happened is we disclosed summaries. Your Honour may recall this. And the matter reemerged on the 17th of October after General Talic had been taken ill and there were various applications. One of the problems which I accepted full responsibility for was that we had delayed, and there was an explanation given, in turning over the Rule 68 material in one of the interviews, and also the interviews that had been conducted for the Stakic case. I provided an explanation that it was an oversight, and Your Honours accepted it. But Your Honours, it was quite a heated exchange that day. And one of the things that was argued, apart from the fact it was suggested we deliberately delayed in disclosing it, was whether or not we should be turning over the whole interview as opposed to the Rule 68, and also whether that should be in summary form or reproduced in the exact words used. And Your Honour, one of the things that was said by Mr. Ackerman at page 10929 of the transcript, when asking for the actual words, was: "The Prosecution has a right to redact and only to supply those parts of the transcript that are Rule 68 material." Now, Your Honour, before Your Honours issued the judgement which was on the 30th of October, I had a conversation with Mr. Ackerman in the course of which I asked whether he was seeking the whole transcripts as opposed to just the Rule 68 material. And his response was no, it was the Rule 68 material properly recorded that he wished to have. Your Honours then gave a ruling on the 30th of October, and there was reference to the Rutaganda decision because we at that stage wondered whether it might have an affect, and the Defence said they didn't seek to argue, take it any further, other than the Rule 68, and that's what you ruled that we should supply. And I don't think there's any dispute now that we did supply the actual transcripts. Now, Your Honour, what's now happened is this, as Your Honours have seen: That the Defence are now calling and proposing to call persons who the Office of the Prosecutor interviewed. We, as Your Honours have seen, are using those interviews to test the veracity and thereby the credibility of those witnesses because, Your Honours, of course, you have to carry out a truth-seeking exercise. And it's our submission that by seeing what the witnesses say, and then comparing it to what they said in interview, you are able to perhaps see where the truth lies. We have been providing the full transcript before cross-examination begins, or occasionally when it's started before a break, at the break, without objection so far or further application until yesterday. And I understand from Mr. Ackerman's remark yesterday that it's because I said we wouldn't supply it. The fact is he hasn't made any application, or the Defence haven't, since October of last year to have the full transcripts. Now, Your Honour, it's our submission there's no rule which requires us to turn over the full transcripts unless it's -- there's a submission that it falls within the purview of Rule 66 B. Your Honour, reciprocal disclosure was invoked by Mr. Ackerman way back in this case with the only request being that we turn over the Banja Luka documents. Your Honour, reciprocity is a two-way thing. Now, the Defence have not turned over to us statements from the witnesses they're calling. We have those short, sometimes lengthened summaries. Your Honour will recall that Mr. Cunningham, when pointed out that the witness could refresh his memory from any statements said they were not taking statements and we had not been provided with any sort of proofing documents as a result of proofing. Your Honour, equally, as Your Honour heard yesterday, certainly witnesses such as Mr. Radic have been turning over documents to the Defence which haven't been supplied to us either. So, Your Honour, if there's going to be reciprocity, it has to be a two-way thing, and you can't say, well, we've never taken statements so there's nothing we can give you. Your Honour, in the spirit of cooperation, and I've made this suggestion to Mr. Ackerman, we are prepared to turn over the full transcript once the witness begins his examination-in-chief. In other words, after proofing. Your Honour, we do this so that Mr. Ackerman can see the full -- or Mr. Cunningham can see the full interview at a stage when the witness is still in-chief, but we're anxious to avoid the -- put it this way, the witness being given a chance to tailor what he wished to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. say in the light of what is contained in the interviews. Your Honour, that's the suggestion I made. I understand from Mr. Ackerman it's not acceptable, and he wants to have the interviews supplied in advance of each of the witnesses coming to testify. So Your Honours, what we're doing is seeking a ruling from you on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two questions, Ms. Korner: Would the individual, the witness, like Mr. Radic, have been at any time provided with a copy of his interview with you, with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. That's number one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All that I understand he was provided with was the Rule 68, which is very lengthy. I mean, it runs to about 24 pages, I think in the first interview, and something like 15 for the second. I imagine -- and you know, he was, I believe from what Mr. Ackerman said shown that when he was proofed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's shown the document by Mr. Ackerman himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The second thing: How do you reconcile what the substance of your submission with the fact that the witness would be, apart from you and your office, would be the only person to hopefully remember what the substance of the interview was all about and what he stated. So assuming that that is the case, how would it change if disclosing or making available the entire statement or interview before the examination-in-chief starts, how do you reconcile the two? Because the witness would, I suppose, know exactly what is contained in the statement in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, he might, Your Honour, depending on if he remembered what he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic probably wouldn't remember, but Mr. Radic would.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic clearly, from what Your Honour says, has a very good recollection of what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In Banja Luka in 2001. Your Honour is right to say, that Mr. Radic -- he informed us that he had been seen by the Defence on I think two occasions before he actually spoke to us. Your Honour, the situation is this: Your Honour, if witnesses are coming here to tell the truth, leaving aside problems with memory, then this shouldn't cause any problem. Your Honour, if they're not, and Your Honour has seen, I think, perhaps clear examples of not memory failure but actual contradiction --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was when the Prosecution's witnesses were testifying, I think. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine so because we've only heard three of your witnesses so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I accept entirely that Mr. Ackerman was able to use the statements, all of which were provided to him, to cross-examine our witnesses, and there were certainly differences. But Your Honour, that's the situation, and that is why we say really, we're entitled to say that we don't have to turn them over until such time as we use them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just wanted to see your point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the point. I should add, there's one difference: Those who were interviewed as suspects, and this was at a later stage when it became abundantly clear that -- Your Honour, we began these interviews at a stage when the full picture was not clear. Later on it became clearer, and so they were treated as suspects. In those cases, each of the interviewees was given a copy of the tape. So that's the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So I thank you, Ms. Korner. Mr. Ackerman, your remarks, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I requested these transcripts yesterday. I believe I had requested them before on at least three occasions. But in any event, I don't want to get into fighting over what happened in the past. That's not important to me. What's important to me is that I'm requesting them now. Rule 66(B) is fairly clear: "The Prosecutor shall on request permit the Defence to inspect any books, documents, photographs, and tangible objects in the Prosecutor's custody or control which are material to the preparation of the Defence." Now, these are documents in the control of the Prosecutor. They are clearly material to the preparation of the Defence. They deal with exactly the issues we're dealing with here. They deal with the crisis staff. They deal with the police. They deal with the military. They deal all of these municipalities that we're dealing with. Nothing could be more material to the preparation of the Defence than these interviews. The second problem is that now that two of them have been turned over to us, Mr. Blagojevic and Mr. Radic, it's clear that the Prosecutor's view of what is Rule 68 material is excessively conservative because we have found in all these statements large swaths of material that should have been turned over under Rule 68. We have not raised it because what good would it do to raise it and ask you to sanction the Prosecutor. There's not much you could do but order them to give us the rest of it. So I think in the interest of justice and in the interest of enforcing Rule 66(B) you should order this material be turned over rather immediately. Ms. Korner -- what Ms. Korner wants to do, and she was very up-front about it, is she is hoping some of these people will not remember what they said in the interviews and say something different in court so she could then confront them with what they said in the interviews and make them look like they're being untruthful rather than forgetful. That would be helpful to the Prosecution. I understand that. But I don't think it's in the spirit of or even in the language of Rule 66(B). Regard to the witnesses turning over documents to us, we are required and will on every occasion give the Prosecutor any documents we're going to use in the defence of the case. But we don't have to turn over any document that any witness might give us. That's nowhere in the rules and anything else. We won't do that. And the Prosecutor won't do that either. It's not usual that these witnesses give us documents anyway how. There have only been a handful. With regard to witness statements, we have a very limited number of witness statements because we just didn't have the -- well, because we didn't take them. But I think we even brought one today to turn over to the Prosecutor. I believe we did. We have a few, a limited number of witness statements. And when we have witness statements, we'll turn them over. We have been spending a large part of the last couple of days working on more detailed summaries, and I think we're nearly prepared to turn those over if we haven't already. So that's all proceeding. But I don't think there's any argument that would allow the Prosecutor to not honour the requirements under Rule 66(B) and turn over this material, that is material in preparation for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to add anything, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. First of all, Rule 66(B), if you recall it does apply, because it doesn't talk about statements. It talks about books, documents, photographs, and tangible objects. Now, Your Honour, I don't particularly want to rely on that, because I know there's been no real ruling on this from the Appeals Chamber. It is a question of argument even within our office as to whether it applies to statements, so I don't want to push that. What I do say, Your Honour, is this: It's wrong if Mr. Ackerman says because they forget. Your Honour, are they telling the truth in the evidence they're giving? Clearly there's a difference between forgetting what happened and actually giving a diametrically opposed description. Your Honour, that's all I want to say. Your Honour, in our submission, we're being very open about the fact we're prepared to turn it over once examination-in-chief starts. But as I say, if Your Honour orders that we turn it over earlier, then we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The statements or the transcript of the interviews with Mr. Radic have been handed to the Defence already, now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They were handed as soon as the first break -- and in fact when cross-examination started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In their entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In their entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We would like to have a copy of them, too. Next witness that will be coming Friday, has he ever been interviewed?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So there is no urgency on our part to decide the matter today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we can discuss it amongst ourselves, and we'll come back on it on -- sometime next week. One thing I wanted to tell you, Mr. Ackerman, is this: That you are right in reading Rule 67(C), that the right of reciprocal disclosure or the duty of reciprocal disclosure contemplated there does not give the Prosecution the right to ask to inspect all the documents that you may have in your archives. But only those which you intend to use as evidence in the trial. You are a hundred per cent right. The only problem that exists is the problem that you yourself have created because as we go along, you're only discovering from day to day which documents you will be making use as evidence in the case. And until last week, there were very few documents that you were aware of that you intended to make use of. And I don't think we can approach the matter of reciprocal disclosure using such yardsticks. So I don't want to prolong this any further. If you have any remarks now, very concisely, I would invite you to come forward with them. And the matter will rest there, and we'll come with our decision later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I will say this: It's still on my number one priority to finish getting through the documents. And contrary to the way the Prosecutor is treating Rule 68, I am erring on the side of being very liberal with regard to these documents. If there's a chance in the world we are going to use them, I am turning them over. If you look at the documents, you'll see there are documents that I've turned over. It's probably unlikely that they're going to be used, but I wanted to err on the side of turning them over rather than the side of holding them back and saying later that I changed my mind because I've already come under criticism for not getting them turned over as quickly as I should have. I'm still working through them as fast as I can. We're increasing the list every week. And so I think we're close to the end of that process. And I think within another -- I hope before we depart for Banja Luka to have that finished and have everything turned over by them, that we have at the present time at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just mention one thing as a matter of administration about the statements, just to make it absolutely clear -- the interview transcripts. There are three sets unfortunately. The first set of transcripts is the English that is spoken on the tape. In other words, the question in English and the interpreter's reply from the person being interviewed. However, because in particular of what happened with I think it was -- not Mr. Blagojevic, but the witness before, maybe it was Mr. Blagojevic, we're checking as to whether or not what was said in B/C/S was correctly interpreted. Occasionally, luckily nothing very bad, there are, because of the constraints of a very quick interview, there are things that are said that are slightly incorrectly interpreted. So there's a second English version which shows what the witness actually said interpreted into English by an interpreter here. But that's not what appears on the English in the actual interview. And then there's a third version which is the B/C/S taken direct from the tape. Your Honour, what we're going to give you, and although we gave Mr. Ackerman yesterday a corrected version, it's easier to follow if you see the straight English rather than with highlighted corrections as I said when it came up on the screen yesterday. We'll arrange for copies to be made, but they are also available which will be given to Mr. Ackerman and we have them ourselves in hard copy a correction just in case the B/C/S was incorrectly interpreted. So if that's satisfactory, what will be handed to Your Honours is what Mr. Ackerman has got or will get, is the original version, which is the English as spoken in the interview. Sorry, it's a bit complicated, but that's the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll sleep on this. The only thing that I would suggest is this: That you're both very experienced lawyers, and if you juxtapose what is contained in Rule 66(A) and Rule 66(B) together with what is provided in 67(C) and not come to a short of an amicable arrangement between you, you will be putting the Trial Chamber in a position where we have to decide whether there is overall a distinction between books, documents, photographs, and tangible objects in the possession of either of you, and statements which are referred to specifically in 66(A)(ii) putting us in a position where we will be in quite a significant legal issue. And frankly, I don't know if we have sufficient time to do that as we go along because these witnesses will be coming over within relatively a very short time. The only advantage that there is is that there's going to be this ten-day interval when the Defence team will be in Bosnia, and we could possibly use that time to draw up a decision. But if we could avoid having to do that, we would appreciate that. That would entail, of course, some kind of an agreement between you. I don't know how many of the witnesses that we will be having were actually interviewed by the Prosecution. If it's not a major problem, maybe you can --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not a huge number, Your Honour, as far as I know. But equally one of the things, and that's why it should only be decided when we know that the witness is actually coming. You already heard from Mr. Ackerman that somebody on the list, somebody we have already interviewed, and that's Mr. Kupresanin, is not coming or may not be coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has lost his way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. We have been able to assist the Defence with that. We provided him with a phone number where we are able to reach him ourselves. Your Honour, the only difficulty I mean it's not a real difficulty as such is that it's not a reciprocal rule because the Rule clearly says we're only entitled to inspect anything they intend to use. Well, if they're going to use it, we're going to get it anyhow, so it doesn't help us to inspect it. And it's not the same thing as them being able to say "we want to inspect everything or anything that you've got, which we say is relevant." So it's not a -- an equality of arms rule. For once, it's in the favour of the Defence, as I'm sure Mr. Ackerman will be the first to admit. Your Honour, I think we rather do want a ruling. It is a situation that's arisen in other Trial Chambers and other cases and it has never been resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's probably because it's a little bit -- not odious, but I want to find a milder way of describing it. Ms. Korner, there's no question, there is no doubt that Rule 66(A)(ii) is referring to the statements of those witnesses that the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That we're going to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- That the Prosecution is going to call. And there's nothing provided for statements released or given to you by other persons that you decide not to bring forward. Except Rule 68, which then binds you to disclose to the Defence. This is why I'm saying that -- I don't know anyway, if you want a decision, we will give you a decision. But I think the other Chambers that did not give a decision took the right Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. This case is proving a milestone for a number of things, and I don't think it has ever arisen in such an acute form as this before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I'm suggesting that if it is acute, it would be acute if we're talking of practically the majority of the witnesses of the Defence having already released -- been interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor, as prospective witnesses or as suspects and having released a statement. That would indeed be acute. But apart from Mr. Radic and Mr. Blagojevic, there are a couple of other witnesses, maybe four in all, that I don't even know if they have been interviewed by the Prosecution. If it's the case of maybe only three or four witnesses, then I suggest that you try and find a solution modus vivendi between you, or amongst you rather than put pressure and have the matter decided. Let it be decided where the problem is indeed acute.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's simply this: We say is our suggestion is we give it to them when examination-in-chief starts. Or after proofing. Mr. Ackerman says no, we want it before proofing. That's the real divide. It's not that we're refusing to turn them over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Cunningham next time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So, you know, short of Mr. Cunningham becoming lead counsel, that's where we are at the moment. Well, Your Honour, as I say, in fact I don't think any of the witnesses next week are coming -- who are coming --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour can I also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- One further request, and that is if any of the witnesses who are coming potentially Friday and next week have made statements to the Defence, could we have them or could we have proper summaries because we've only got the three line or the rather inadequate ones at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think I have anything with regard to the next witness, Mr. Ackerman, not even a summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That is going to be my job. I thought there was one for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is the standard, very short, six line or seven line or three line in the original document that you had submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Then I will have one for the next three witnesses, if you give me your email Ms. Korner, I will have them probably by the start of business tomorrow. And I'll have a copy delivered to you early --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't give you mine, because if I do in open session, I will start receiving a lot of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in response to Mr. Cunningham, it can be emailed to Ms. Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And if it's not to your satisfaction, Ms. Korner, please draw my attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's bring in Mr. Radic to tell us whether he ever thought he could be indicted here. Never crossed his mind he said yesterday, didn't he? We will sit according to the schedule that we adopted the day before yesterday, if that is okay with you, also because I was sitting right through half past 1.00 today, and I don't want to overtire myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say, when I last night went through the matter I need to deal with Mr. Radic, it's quite clear it's going to go into Friday. Just so that Mr. Ackerman knows as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was originally meant to be so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, if the next witness turns up tomorrow -- tomorrow, if he turns up tomorrow, would it be possible -- I don't know, it's up to you. You are the one who can actually help us decide. You know that we are sitting Friday afternoon. There is a possibility, great possibility, that we could shift the sitting to Friday morning. But I would take it that you would need time to proof the witness. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm just wondering if we shouldn't try to stop him if he hasn't already left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not up to me. I mean, to me it's pretty obvious that Mr. Radic is going to be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Otherwise, he'll be stuck here through the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But it's not within my power to stop him. I mean, it's -- he is your witness, and I think you have to tie up with whoever is responsible to stop him coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we'll try to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. In which case we would be able to shift the sitting to the morning?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I'm concerned, I just have explained to somebody that a meeting that was due to be held in the afternoon should go to the morning, but I'm sure we can go back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, just let me know. Because I wouldn't like to disturb --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as we're concerned, that's fine, if you want to sit in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So I thank you. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Radic. Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My apologies to you on behalf of the Trial Chamber for having kept you waiting for the past three-quarters of an hour. This was due to procedural matters that we needed to discuss, which you are not involved, you have nothing to do with them. But they needed to be discussed, and this was the only occasion and the first occasion that we had to deal with them. So my apologies to you once more. I'm sure that you understand. Ms. Korner is going to proceed with her cross-examination of you, which I anticipate will not finish neither today nor tomorrow, from the looks of it. So be prepared to be here also on Friday. But if you keep your answers to what is necessary, short in particular, and precise, I think you stand a good chance of being home by the end of the week. Thank you. Ms. Korner, he is in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Ms. Korner: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I want to deal in a general form, please, with the governmental authority structure in the Serbian Republic. Do you understand what I mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, can we deal with the structure of the SDS before effectively the SDS became the government. There was the main board, and underneath the main board there were municipal boards. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And within the municipalities, certain, if I can put it that way, villages also had their own boards, is that right, which reported to the municipal boards?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were organisational branches at lower levels which were -- had to respond to municipal boards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in its turn, the municipal boards responded to the main board?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, originally, there was no intervening regional structure. Is that right? But that was set up effectively through 1991, from about the middle of 1991, and lasted until September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't confirm that exactly. But there was some sort of a regional connection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am receiving it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, instead of turning it up, I turned it down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Well do you remember -- well, if we look at it this way, we had first of all in the Krajina region the association of Bosnian Krajina municipalities set up in April of 1991.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In September of 1991, it became -- that organisation became the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That organisation established the assembly. It didn't become an assembly, but they established the ARK Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you, in fact, were a member, both of the -- a delegate to the association of municipalities and a representative to the Assembly of the Autonomous Region? That's right, isn't it? I can show you the document if you like.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please show me the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I knew you would say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you have a look, please, at P61. I've got it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you turn, please, Mr. Radic to -- I've lost it now. Sorry. Yes, it's number 97 on the list. If you can put it on the ELMO. Do you see your name there?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's 97, 114, 94, but perhaps a page is missing. I don't have page number 5 before me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Could you look at number 97, which should be the third page of the list.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I wasn't aware that there was something on the other side, too. 97, here it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Mr. Radic, why can't you just tell us that you were a member, that you were a delegate to the Assembly of the Autonomous Region instead of looking at a document?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the simple reason that I was rarely present in ARK Assembly. And later on, I will tell you why. But by virtue of their positions, all presidents of municipal assemblies were also members, even the vice-president, Slobodan Boskovic. They were also assembly members. That's what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm sure that -- Mr. Radic, all that I'm asking you is not why or how, but the fact that you were a member. And indeed, I can show you a number of documents. You were there right at the early stages. Could you have a look, please, at P11. This is the session of the 14th of May 1991. This was the meeting about the statute of the autonomous region. And if you look under item 2, you made various remarks about the statute. So do you agree you were there then?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the first session. The second session, yes. Item 2, and 1. Item 2, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you made remarks that the statute proposed was too short, should be a draft brought up for public debate, and all of that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Now, I don't actually want to get sidetracked into your part for the moment. I want to deal with the general principles of the power structures. So you can give the document back to the usher. Thank you. Now, the assembly of the autonomous region was proclaimed on the 16th of September 1991. And I'd be grateful if you take the date from me, Mr. Radic. And do you remember that on the 21st of November at the second session of the Serbian Assembly in Bosnia-Herzegovina, what was called the autonomous regions, the Serb Autonomous Regions, were all verified?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you could show me a document that I can refresh my memory, I would be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which for the 16th of October or --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to whether I remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Or for the 21st of November?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the 21st of November, when you said that there was an assembly and that delegates, all delegates were present then. I'd like to see that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't expecting to show this. Can I just ask Ms. Gustin to check what the exhibit number is. I think it may be 35. I'm not a hundred per cent sure. P17, we think. Actually, give it to me first, and then we can give it to the witness. 17, 1-7, sorry. Yes, thank you. All right. We need to find -- that's the English. Usher, I don't know how you're going to find the B/C/S, but that's the English. He needs to have the B/C/S. Where is the B/C/S? All right. Usher, can you put that on the ELMO, and we'll find the... All right, we'll see if we can find the...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's disclosure 2249 if that helps in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I need the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have it here on the screen. If the system worked, I could display it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What page in the B/C/S? That's it, I think. Page 31 in the B/C/S version, I think. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you, Mr. Radic, look at that, please, and just confirm.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I ask someone to go and fetch my glasses because they're in my coat pocket in the waiting room. I have two pairs of glasses there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, usher, I don't know how we should go back this. Do you have any other personal belongings there, Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose the best thing would be to have usher escort you, and you bring whatever you need from that room. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two pairs of glasses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether Your Honour wants to explain to Mr. Radic that if we go on like this, he won't be finishing on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I won't be explaining anything to him. I'm going to leave him and you as free as a bird.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you think you're doing me a favour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But Ms. Korner, I mean, we are all experienced. So I know when to step in, and I know when to stay out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm going to try in the hopes that we can...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's wait for Judge Taya who will be with us in a minute. So, in the meantime, Mr. Radic can have a look at the document. Yes, Ms. Korner, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, having seen that, do you accept that on the 21st of November at the second session of the Serbian Republic Assembly, the Serbian Autonomous Regions were verified?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got this document a moment ago. I tried to find out whether I was present at this session. My name is not on the list. I should read the whole document. But if that's what the document says, then the regions must have been verified because from this document I cannot see that I was present at this session, nor that I took part in the discussion. I'm trying to remember, but...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, all right. Mr. Radic, I think if we can try and set some ground rules for this to prevent this becoming even more protracted. First of all, can you take it that if I put to you something happened on a date that exists, unless I particularly want to put it to you, you can take it from me because if I'm wrong Mr. Ackerman and Their Honours will correct me. Do you understand that? Otherwise, if I have to show you a document every time, we will be here forever. Now, the second thing is this: I wasn't asking you whether you were present at the meeting. I was asking you if you were aware or if you agreed with me that on the 21st of November, the Serbian Autonomous Regions were verified. Now, whether you were present at the meeting or not, you knew that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say I did know that. Obviously, if that's what the document says, that they were verified, then that must have been the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And until the constitution was changed in September 1992 when the autonomous regions were abolished, they were part of the governmental structure, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who was part of the governmental structure?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The regions. And if you don't understand what I mean, I'll put it differently. The structure of the authorities in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was as follows: At the top was the republican-level government headed by Karadzic. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what it says, yes. Because I mean, really I cannot say whether Karadzic was the president of the government because elected members of the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina were Mr. Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic. As to what Karadzic was, what position he had, I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that really what you're telling this Court, that you're unable to tell us what position Karadzic held between 1991 November and 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of the SDS. Now, what followed from that, I really couldn't tell you. There should be a document demonstrating what exactly his position was during the period that you're now discussing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to look at a document and I'm not going to show you a document, Mr. Radic. I'm asking you of your own personal knowledge in the position that you held during that period, are you telling us you had no idea what position Mr. Karadzic held?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say one thing. The president of the government, as far as I can recall, was Dr. Branko Dzeric at the time. As to what position Mr. Karadzic had and when it was that the presidency was created, the presidency with Mr. Karadzic as the presiding of that body whose members were also Mr. Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic, that I couldn't tell you because I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm not going to pursue that, Mr. Radic. But I want to go back to the structure. Do you agree whoever, whether it was Koljevic, Plavsic, Karadzic, whoever, that was the republican-level government?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, it is possible that that was the case. However, shortly after that, Mr. Dzeric was elected president of the government. It is true that he did not hold this position for a very long time. But he was the president of the government for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Forgetting whether it was -- I'll include Dzeric in there. Was there a government at the republic level based in Sarajevo-Pale?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could not be based in Sarajevo, only at Pale because at the time when Serbian deputies left the assembly, they went to Pale, and it was only then and there that the government was established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Radic, I'm trying very briefly to establish what the position was about the governmental structures. If you argue about whether it was Pale or Sarajevo, it will take even longer. I'm asking you how the governmental structures worked. So we could go through that, please. Now, next, that was the head, if you like, of the SDS which then became the government of the Serbian Republic. Under that structure, for the period between November 1991 and September 1992, was there the regional authority, particularly in what was then the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot tell you the exact date when the assembly of the ARK was established, when the government was established, and when Mr. Erceg was elected Prime Minister or became Prime Minister-elect. He later on made a proposal to the members of the government of the region. Unfortunately I could not tell you the composition of that government because I was not its member nor was I the member of the government at Pale. I would really like to help you, but I simply don't know. I'm sure you have a list of the members of the government both at the regional and republican level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I'm not interested in who formed these levels of government. Can I make that absolutely clear. I am interested in the structures. Now, do you know what I mean?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean when you say "the structure"? Are you referring to the various departments that existed as part of the government? Is that the structure that you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the levels of authorities within the government of the Serbian Republic. Now, can we go on from there. The regional authorities, forget about the dates if you say you don't know what they were, existed during the that this case is about. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, yes. But please do not tie me to any particular date. There were governments of both Republika Srpska and the region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The regional authorities got their instructions - is this right - and we will look at what you said about this in interview in a moment. But is this right: They got their instructions from the authorities in Pale?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Surely they must have obeyed the instructions that were coming from the republican government. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they passed on those instructions to the municipal level of authorities?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The municipal would report back sometimes to the regional, sometimes to the government in Pale. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, that relationship, the relationship between the regional government and municipal governments, like the relationship between the municipal government and the republican government, at least as far as Banja Luka is concerned, did not function ideally, as perfectly as one would assume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I accept that entirely, Mr. Radic. I accept that there were no rigid chains of command and that things did not always happen in the same way in each municipality. But in general terms, is what I have said to you correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It really depends on the municipality in question and what they expected from the regional government and the government of Republika Srpska. I once said that the state did not function during this initial period of one year the way it should have functioned. At least, the way it had been envisaged. And this concerns in particular the regional government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Can I suggest to you that one of the reasons for having a regional level of government in place, particularly during this period, was that there were difficulties in communication between municipalities in the Krajina and Pale?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the establishment of the regional -- I mean, of the ARK, and later the government and the assembly, was the consequence of a desire to have a greater cooperation amongst these municipalities, Banja Luka, Dubica, Grahovo, Gradiska, and some others. That was the first requirement that had been set out. Later, links were established between regional bodies and bodies at the level of the republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If I use the word "coordinating function," would you agree with that? That was the regional bodies' original function?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that should have been the case. It should have had the coordinating function. However, many municipalities did not accept this coordinating function. I believe I have already mentioned some of them earlier on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because you see, some of these municipalities expected a certain assistance from the level of the region. But I said that regional bodies did not have enough means to offer any material assistance whatsoever, so this coordinating function was not very well received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the simplest thing, Mr. Radic, would be to go through with you what you said about this in the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask if we have up on the screen, please, page 27 of the first interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You'll be able to see it in your own language, Mr. Radic, and we'll look at the English translation.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hardly read --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we enlarge it a little bit?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can't, unfortunately, Mr. Radic. We'll give you the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We think it's this page. Page 28.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was -- I want you to find the part, Mr. Radic, if you can, the question was put to you: "Mr. Brdjanin was a very powerful man, was he not?" And you said this: "I wanted to draw your attention to the fact that power did not come from the crisis staff, which only lasted a brief period. Many of the decisions he made I simply rejected. The power of these people came from higher authorities, from their authorities as deputies, as minister, and things like that."

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Radic --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what page you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, although it's a bit early, I'm going to sort out for the nth time the problem of these transcripts. Would Your Honour care to rise now while I do that because the next few question I have all relate to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any problem with that, Mr. Ackerman? We will rise now have a break of 20 minutes starting from now. And please try to be punctual so we don't waste or lose time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I'd like you now --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope this will never happen again after today, it probably will, but we just have too many versions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- To look at, please, page 24 for us in the English, and we've highlighted the -- what we think is the B/C/S part of it. So if we could have page 24 up on the screen for everyone. Now, Mr. Radic, you were actually being asked about Mr. Brdjanin. Do you see the question: "Mr. Brdjanin was a very powerful man." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the screen or in the text in front of me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the text. Don't worry about the screen, just look at the text. It should have been highlighted for you.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's highlighted in yellow. It says that the power of those people --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Yes. All right. I'm sorry, Mr. Radic, yes, read that part out that's been highlighted.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The power of those people was a result of their higher functions, their functions as deputies, as ministers," and I won't go on to list everything else. That was my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to what has been highlighted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I am. And so what you were saying there was that the authority of Mr. Brdjanin and others in the regional crisis staff came from their positions as deputies and ministers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the authority of Mr. Brdjanin, the previous question was that it was true to say that Mr. Brdjanin was a very powerful man. I said that his authority wasn't a result of him being the president of the crisis staff, it was a result of him of him having a role of a minister, et cetera, and that is where he derived this authority from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period of the crisis staff, the regional crisis staff, he was a deputy to the assembly, but he became a minister in September of 1992. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember when he became a minister, but I know that he was the deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And later, he was the vice-president in the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to look at some other things that you told us about the relationship between the regional crisis staff or government and the republic level. Could you go now, please -- could you be given, please, what is the B/C/S equivalent of, I hope, page 40 in the English version. And this is from the part where you were being asked at this stage, Mr. Radic, about the dismissals.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that? And it was put to you that the order of the crisis staff led to the dismissals, and I'll come back to the actual mechanics later. But you said this: "The balancing instructions came from Pale, the balancing of personnel which was then supposed to be implemented on the field. And it was a reflection on what was happening in the other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And when it came from the higher authority here, then that's what the implementation began." You were asked how you knew about that, that it came from Pale, and you said there is a document. Now, do you agree that's what you said about the euphemism, as you put it, of balancing? That's right, isn't it, Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you while we're on this page, what did you mean by your answer "it was seen by the person who brought it to the crisis staff to be adopted"? Do you mean the person who brought it to the regional crisis staff had seen the original instructions from Pale?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but this is what you were telling us. Who was the person who told you that the instructions came from Pale?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember who told me about this. I know that I was told that differentiation of staff should be implemented and that this should be implemented throughout Republika Srpska, not just in Republika Srpska but also in Sarajevo, in Zagreb, et cetera. And as a result, it was necessary to implement this in our area, too. There must have been a document because I don't think that someone in the crisis staff would have said let's differentiate the staff. I don't think he would have done this on his own initiative. And this is the euphemism I have referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. If you just understand the exercise, Mr. Radic, I'm just taking you through the various aspects of the instructions that arrived. All right. If you go -- if we can just look at the next page, I think you develop that a little bit - page 41. You were telling us, Mr. Radic, that you were going to -- you were going to refuse to implement this in Banja Luka, and it was put to you, you told us, that you were actually present at this meeting because you argued against this conclusion. And is that -- this was the meeting of the regional crisis staff, so that's one of the ones you attended, was it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was opposed to this? You said, JK, you said you were at this meeting because you were opposed to that decision. Yes. Did you see that order from Pale? I said I didn't. But whenever it was necessary to implement something, instructions would arrive from Pale, and it had to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then the question was did Brdjanin do this or Kupresanin? I said I didn't want to guess. But one of them who had connections with Pale did this, one of them who was a deputy or a minister up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. All right. Thank you. First of all, Mr. Radic, this meeting where this order from Pale was discussed was one at which you were present. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's true to say that I attended the meeting or that I just received -- or that I had just received the document, but I didn't agree with this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you told us there that you argued against it. So it's not a difficult question, Mr. Radic. Can we take it from that that you must have been present at this meeting of the regional crisis staff where this order for levelling or standardisation or whatever it was called came from Pale?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that I had to be there, but I don't exclude that possibility. I don't exclude that possibility, you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And do you now recall, and I'm asking you to recall the actual event, somebody coming and saying: "This is what they have ordered from above, and this is how it will be implemented"?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it must have been. Someone received an order, and that's what had to be done. Because that is how they proceeded in all the municipalities of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that is the procedure in the part that is now called the BH Federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, as I said yesterday, for the moment, we'd just like you to concentrate on what happened in the Republika Srpska. All right. Could you now go, please, with luck, I hope, or can you be given page -- the equivalent of our page 57. I'd like to start with page 57, please.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 58.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, not the English. It's the page before the part that was highlighted. Can you find, again, the series of questions where you were being asked again about Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you saying that Mr. Brdjanin had support in Pale? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's the part I want to ask you about. You gave a description of him, much as you've given to this Court, I think. But that you said here that when he needed support for something, he would just go up there and demand support for whatever. And you were asked: "Go where and demand support?" And you said: "Go to Pale and demand support for certain issues, and that went on until they were sick of him and then they kicked him out." Then you were asked about the issues that he was getting support and then you went on to tell us about "balancing of personnel was his idea or came from someone in Pale." I'm going to suggest to you from other documents that I will show you, Mr. Radic, that Mr. Brdjanin was very much the architect of this idea. However, this is what you said: "And then you went on tell us that" -- or rather, this was put to you again that Mr. Brdjanin retained the support of Pale. Then you dealt with this binding order, this is the next page for us, that Karadzic issued... And then this is the part I want to ask you about. You were dealing or it was put to you that he had the authority, didn't he, through his position in the Serb Assembly and through his position as the president of the crisis staff to do these things. And your reply was this: "Of course we were at a lower level for them, the municipal level, and that's how they acted. You will see I don't know who of the deputies you summoned, but you'll see even today they think that they are something better than others because they were elected the one time in 1990 and they continued to rule until 1996. And if they have a masterful leader like Krajisnik, the deputies, he was their president." And you say -- you said this: "Again, I repeat, you are just wasting your time with the crisis staff. Everything was planned from up above." Then it was put to you that although it was planned by Krajisnik and Karadzic and the rest of them, it was put into operation through the medium of the regional crisis staff, and you said: "No, very little to a small degree. You showed me the decisions made, give me the feedback, and I can show you the documents which I presided over and you will see what I refused and rejected." Now, can we break that down, please, Mr. Radic. First of all, that last part, you were saying that you in your municipality effectively went your own way. Is that right? You weren't following the instructions of the regional crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which last part are you referring to? You've read out a lot. First of all you said that you're claiming that Mr. Brdjanin had a lot of support in Pale. Shall we deal with that first of all. That has to do with a decision on prohibiting the exchange of flats and houses. That's on page 58. Shall we deal with this first of all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. I'm sorry. You were talking about -- on this part, nothing to do with the airport and flights. I hope you were looking at the same part that we were. You were dealing here with the balancing of personnel and Mr. Brdjanin going to Pale. Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was supported in Pale. But you claim that Mr. Brdjanin was supported in Pale, that's on page 59. Is that the part you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I hope.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yes, absolutely. But on this occasion, Karadzic issued a decree law. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall we deal with that issue first of all?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I want to deal with first of all your assertion that you in Banja Luka did not implement the decisions of the regional crisis staff. You went your own way. That's what you were telling us, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that on page 59?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I hope. That's what I just read out, and I hoped you were following.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You read out a lot, so I can't answer your question immediately. But first you said "you claim Mr. Brdjanin is supported in Pale." That had to do with the prohibition on exchanging flats and houses. Having Serbs from the federation and non-Serbs in Banja Luka exchange houses and flats. I said that I was opposed to that, and I asked for Mr. Karadzic to comment on this. Karadzic had issued a decree law and said that this had to be done, that such exchanges had to be implemented, and this is what I refused to do first of all. And then we have JK, never asked anyone for anything because he had authority as a member --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. That's right. Don't bother about reading out the questions. I've read it out. You've read it. I just want to concentrate and summarise what you're saying there. Do you understand that, Mr. Radic? You were saying two things, or three things really. First, as you told us, the question of the housing and Karadzic's binding order. And you dealt with that. Second, you were saying that the municipal level was at a lower level, and that the deputies, that is to say people like Krajisnik and whatever who were strong, were sending out orders -- sorry, were planning things at their level. That's what you were saying there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's something else. So forget about what I said above about the decree law issued by Mr. Karadzic, and we'll refer to the part which starts with "we were a lower municipal level for them, and that is how they behaved." Is that what you're asking me about now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exactly. But I don't need you to read it all out, Mr. Radic. Everybody's read it. I'm just asking you if that's what you were saying in terms. In other words, if it was people at the level of deputies, like Krajisnik, like Karadzic, and like Mr. Brdjanin, who were planning these matters which then were given as orders to the municipal levels?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wanted to say is quite clear in the text. I said that the deputies thought that they were more important than people at the municipal level, and that is how they behaved. I said if they had such a masterful leader such as Krajisnik, it resulted from all of this. I never mentioned Karadzic as someone who participated in this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, finally, were you saying on this page, and then we can move on, that you were not in your municipality, in Banja Luka, carrying out the orders of the regional crisis staff? Is that what you were saying there?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the ones that weren't in accordance with the law and the rules, my secretary would forward them to me and said this can't be implemented. And these things weren't implemented. There were certain illogical matters, too. For example, when a woman from Visoko contacted me, she had a house there which she wanted exchanged and there was a Bosniak who wanted to do that. But there were rules, and Karadzic sorted this out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would carry out anything that you thought was in accordance with the law. Do you mean by that the law of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you something. Many laws, in addition to the laws of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I will apply many of the laws from the SFRJ period. These laws were still applied. They had not been abolished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you applied the old laws as well as the laws that were passed by the Serbian Republic. Is that the situation?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The laws adopted by the National Assembly of Republika Srpska, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we look, please, then at one more aspect of life in Banja Luka that I think was affected by --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just trying to find, because of the difference in page numbers... Yes, can we go, please, to -- can you be shown, and we have up on the screen I think page 68. And we'll give you the -- yes. The B/C/S version. I'm sorry, Mr. Radic, we haven't found it yet. Can you give it back to us, please. Yes, thank you. It's page 69.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were being asked there: "What was the purpose as you understand it of destroying mosques?" And you said: "The same as the destruction of orthodox churches, to destroy the faith so that people wouldn't go back. Destroy the spiritual basis, and they won't be coming back. It's crazy." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just find it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd be grateful if you told me it was under number 22. If you told me it was under number 2, I would have found it more easily. What's the purpose? Because it's the same reason for which orthodox churches are destroyed, and the purpose was to prevent people from returning. Yes, that's what I said. And finally at the end, I said: "It's madness."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now you went on, and you can read it to yourself, to explain that you were being blamed by the Serbs because you tried to prevent the mosques being destroyed.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was Serb policy to blow up mosques, and you were trying to prevent it. Is that what you're -- what you were saying there and what you still say now?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You won't find any such explicitly defined policies, and I didn't find them anywhere. But this went without saying because all orthodox churches had previously been destroyed in Croatia, all of them. And that was the answer. Destroying all the mosques in the territory of the Republic of Serbia. These policies were never stated in such an explicit manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But according to you, you knew this was wrong.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. That's why I was opposed to it, and that's why Banja Luka came last, defended itself until 1993. I have to inform this Trial Chamber that up until that time -- by that time, all the mosques had been destroyed in the territory of Republika Srpska. Banja Luka came last unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. The actual destruction came in 1993, although attacks had been made on the mosques in 1992. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in Banja Luka. But other towns in Republika Srpska, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. You misunderstand me. I don't mean that they were destroyed, but there had been attempts to damage already in 1992 the mosques in Banja Luka. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they failed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you went on -- I want you to read on, please, to yourself about what else you said in relation to these --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's all right. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you just read on to yourself and come to the part where you said -- I asked you who was talking to you about blowing up mosques. And you said: "Everybody, even those in highest authority. They were explaining. They always said `Radic, Banja Luka's fine. You're doing well. The only problem is you still have mosques there.'" And you talked about taking the Russian Ambassador to look at the mosque. Can you read on. You were asked: "Who do you mean by people higher up?" And you said: "They all said it. Don't ask me for names. From the highest authority all the way down to the lowest." You were asked: "Does it include Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik?" And your reply: "They are wise enough not to say it out loud, but they had their emissaries who they sent here all the time, and one of them was especially persistent." You were asked: "Who was that?" And you eventually -- you began by saying: "Ask the CSB and the judges. They know everything." You were asked again to tell us who it was who had been sent. And did you then say: "Ostojic, Velibor Ostojic, was on my back all the time." You were asked about him. And the interview continued. He said -- I'm sorry, you said that he held a high position, that he was a deputy, and that he was effectively -- you were asked: "And whose back was he on?" And you said: "Mostly mine." You were questioned: "Because of your stance against the destruction of the mosques. Correct"? Not only that I kept defying them, and you dealt with the coup, or the attempted coup in 1993. And then the -- Mr. Ostojic coming down to Banja Luka. Now, was all of that true?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what sense more or less? Is there anything you want to change?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that he came to issue directives. But there were talks about that. He said: "You're doing fine. Everybody's okay in Banja Luka, it's just that the mosques are still standing." There were others as well who kept coming. Those who had done the job before, they were the ones who constantly suggested to us and kept telling us that this had to be done. Of course, this was done without the knowledge of the municipal government, which is what I already described at the time it happened, that it was sheer madness which would eventually cost the Serbian People very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. It's taken -- I'm sorry it has taken such a long time to go through this, Mr. Radic, because of the difficulties with the interview. But is this the position generally: That orders, planning and orders, originated in Pale?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what planning you're talking about. The plan to destroy places of worship or...?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, generally the policies to be carried out within the territories of what was proclaimed to be the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the policy had to start from the top. It is at the top that the general principles are defined and then transmitted down the chain of command. This is how it was done within the federation and elsewhere during the war. This is not something new.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Again, I'm not suggesting that it was any different anywhere else, but I just want to deal with what happened in the Serbian Republic. It was transmitted down the chain of command. That chain of command included the regional, the municipal, and then the local communes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
